name: Jorepokhri
tagline: Twin ponds, India's first salamander sanctuary and an honest update
meta_description: Jorepokhri near Darjeeling: India's first salamander sanctuary (1985), why the newts no longer breed there, the GTA lodge, Mim tea, fares and best months.
summary: Jorepokhri is a pair of small ponds at about 2,250 m, 4 km from Sukhia Pokhari and about 20 km from Darjeeling. In 1985 it became India's first salamander sanctuary, for the Himalayan newt, but recent reporting says the newts no longer breed in its altered ponds. Come for a quiet forest stop, the story and the state lodge.

local_story.title: The twin ponds and the newt that left
paras: Jore pokhri is Nepali for twin ponds, and that is exactly what you find: two small pools in a fold of forest above Sukhia Pokhari, with conifers around them and mist most afternoons. For decades this was one of the best-known breeding sites in India of the Himalayan salamander, a dark, warty newt with orange markings, now named Tylototriton himalayanus and earlier called T. verrucosus. It spends most of the year hidden in damp ground and leaf litter, and comes to still, shallow water to breed when the rains arrive.

In 1985 the ponds and their surroundings were declared the Jore Pokhri Wildlife Sanctuary, India's first sanctuary created for a salamander. It is tiny, but it mattered: an amphibian, not a tiger or a rhino, got its own protected area. Over the following decades the site was also developed as a tourist spot, with paved paths, railings, concrete edges and buildings around the water. Each change looked like an improvement for visitors. For a newt that needs soft, weedy margins and damp ground, each one took something away.

That is where the honest part of the story begins. Reporting by Mongabay in 2026 found that concrete paving and tourist infrastructure have altered the ponds so much that salamanders are no longer found breeding in the sanctuary. The animal survives in other ponds in the hills, among them Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, Pokhritar and Panch Pokhri. We still think Jorepokhri is worth a stop, but as a lesson in how protection can go wrong and a quiet forest pond, not as a place to see a newt.

did_you_know: Jore Pokhri Wildlife Sanctuary was declared in 1985 as India's first sanctuary created for a salamander, the Himalayan newt Tylototriton himalayanus, earlier called T. verrucosus.
Mongabay reported in 2026 that concrete paving and tourist works have changed Jorepokhri's ponds so much that salamanders are no longer found breeding in the sanctuary.
Jore pokhri means 'twin ponds' in Nepali. The Himalayan newt still breeds in other hill ponds, including Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, Pokhritar and Panch Pokhri.
intro: Jorepokhri is a small place with a big lesson. The twin ponds sit in forest at about 2,250 m, 4 km from Sukhia Pokhari, and the GTA's tourist lodge stands beside them. Most visitors stop for half an hour between Darjeeling and Mirik, walk around the water, read the signs about the salamander and drive on. On a misty afternoon, with the conifers dripping and nobody else around, it is a quietly lovely spot, and a cheap night out of Darjeeling for anyone who wants silence more than sights.

We are honest about the newts. This was India's first salamander sanctuary, declared in 1985, but recent reporting says the animals no longer breed in the ponds after years of concrete and tourist works. If you want to understand the Himalayan salamander, ask locally about the ponds where it survives, such as Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, and treat Jorepokhri as the start of the story. Combine it with Sukhia Pokhari, Lepchajagat, the Mim tea garden and the Simana viewpoint for a full, easy day.

highlights.title: The twin ponds
highlights.text: Two small pools in a fold of conifer forest, with a path around them that takes ten minutes to walk. They are best early or in the mist, when few people are about. Read the boards on the salamander, then look at how hard edges have replaced the soft margins newts once needed.

highlights.title: An honest conservation story
highlights.text: India's first salamander sanctuary, declared in 1985, and a place where, by 2026 reporting, the newts no longer breed. It is worth seeing for that reason: a small site that shows how tourist works can undo protection. Ask locals where the newts survive now.

highlights.title: Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge
highlights.text: The GTA lodge stands beside the ponds and is the one place to sleep right here in the forest. Rooms are simple and the setting very quiet after the day visitors leave. Book through GTA tourism and check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Mim tea estate
highlights.text: The Mim tea garden lies close to Jorepokhri. The road through it gives wide views over tea rows and ridges, and few visitors walk it. Walk a stretch through the bushes and watch the pluckers at work in season, from March to November.

highlights.title: Sukhia Pokhari market
highlights.text: Four kilometres away, Sukhia Pokhari is the local market town and jeep junction. Have momos and tea, watch the jeeps load for Mirik and Maneybhanjan, and buy fruit, snacks or a warm hat for the cold evening back at the ponds.

highlights.title: Simana viewpoint
highlights.text: On the Mirik road beyond Sukhia, Simana looks west across the border into the Ilam hills of Nepal, with Pashupati market at Pashupatinagar just across. A good stop on the way to Mirik, best in clear weather from October to April.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep from Darjeeling's motor stand toward Sukhia Pokhari or Mirik, ₹70–100 a seat and about an hour. From Sukhia Pokhari, Jorepokhri is about 4 km: walk it in an hour or hire a local car for ₹400–700 return with waiting time.
A half-day from Darjeeling covering Lepchajagat, Sukhia Pokhari and Jorepokhri costs ₹1,500–2,500. Mirik day tours from Darjeeling can usually add Jorepokhri if you ask when you book.
From Mirik, shared jeeps toward Darjeeling go via Simana and Sukhia Pokhari. Get off at Sukhia and take a local car for the last 4 km, or walk it.

where_to_stay: The one stay at the ponds is Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge, run by the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration's tourism department. It is simple, quiet and in the forest, with the ponds a few steps away; book through GTA tourism, and check current status and rates before you travel, since booking systems change. Otherwise, stay at nearby Lepchajagat, a short drive back toward Ghoom, where the WBFDC resort and village homestays charge around ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals, or in Darjeeling, about an hour away. Most people simply visit on a day trip from Darjeeling or on the way to Mirik.
tips: Do not come expecting to see salamanders, because recent reporting says they no longer breed in the sanctuary ponds.
Visit early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when tour groups have gone and the forest is quiet.
Stay on paths, keep back from the water's edge and never handle any amphibian you find.
Combine Jorepokhri with Lepchajagat, Sukhia Pokhari and Simana for a full day, since the ponds alone take under an hour.
Bring a warm layer and a rain jacket, because at about 2,250 m afternoons turn cold and misty fast, even in May.

experiences.title: Walk around the twin ponds of Jorepokhri
experiences.summary: An unhurried hour around the two small ponds that gave Jorepokhri its name, with conifer forest, mist and the signboards of India's first salamander sanctuary. Go knowing the newts no longer breed here, and look at why.
body: The walk itself is short: a path loops around both ponds and the forest edge in about ten minutes, and you could be back in the car within half an hour. Do not rush it. The ponds sit in a hollow of tall conifers at around 2,250 m, and early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the day visitors have gone, the place is still and quiet. Mist drifts across the water, forest birds call from the trees, and you can hear the drip from the branches.

Read the boards about the Himalayan salamander, the dark, warty newt for which this became India's first salamander sanctuary in 1985. Then look at the ponds themselves. A newt needs soft, vegetated margins, damp leaf litter and shallow still water to breed and shelter. Here, as Mongabay reported in 2026, concrete paving and tourist works have changed the edges and surroundings so much that salamanders are no longer found breeding in the sanctuary. Seeing that difference for yourself is the real lesson of the visit.

Stay on the paths, keep children back from the water and do not throw food or anything else into the ponds. If you find any amphibian on a path in the wet season, leave it where it is; handling harms their skin. Carry a warm layer and a rain jacket, because the weather changes fast at this height. Then walk on along the Mim tea road, or drive the 4 km down to Sukhia Pokhari for momos and tea.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: There may be a small entry or parking fee collected at the site, set by the authorities and liable to change. It has never been an expensive stop. Carry small notes, and if you are staying at the GTA lodge you are already beside the water. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: Thirty minutes to an hour for the ponds themselves, longer if you want to sit quietly or walk the forest road. Most people combine it with Sukhia Pokhari, Lepchajagat and Simana in a half or full day from Darjeeling, or stop on the way to Mirik.

faqs.q: Why did the salamanders stop breeding at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: According to 2026 reporting by Mongabay, the ponds were altered by concrete paving and tourist infrastructure, which replaced the soft, vegetated edges and damp ground the newts depend on. The species survives in other hill ponds, such as Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, Pokhritar and Panch Pokhri.

experiences.title: Walk the Mim tea garden road
experiences.summary: A morning walk from Jorepokhri along the road through the Mim tea garden, with tea rows falling away below, pluckers at work in season and wide views over the ridges. Easy walking, no ticket and none of the crowds of the gardens near town.
body: Mim is one of the Darjeeling tea gardens on the ridge around Sukhia Pokhari and Jorepokhri, a part of the district far fewer visitors see than the gardens of Kurseong or Darjeeling town. The road through it winds across steep slopes of tea bushes, shade trees and small workers' settlements. In the plucking season, from March to November, the bushes are worked in the morning by teams of women who pick two leaves and a bud by hand and carry them in baskets on their backs.

Start from Jorepokhri after breakfast and walk down the garden road, or ask your driver to drop you a few kilometres in and collect you lower down. Keep to the road and main paths, which the garden's own people use, and do not step into the rows. If you want to photograph pluckers up close, ask first and accept a no. A factory visit is not something to count on; if you are keen, ask at the garden office, and remember that work comes first in the busy flush seasons.

First flush, in March and April, gives the light, flowery Darjeeling teas that fetch the highest prices; second flush, in May and June, is fuller and more muscatel; the monsoon months bring the most leaf and the greenest slopes. Each looks different on the bushes. Carry water and a rain jacket, and wear shoes with grip, because the road is steep in parts. If you want to buy the garden's tea, Darjeeling's tea shops are the surest place to find a labelled packet.

faqs.q: Can we visit the Mim tea factory?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it is not a tourist factory with fixed tours. Ask at the garden office, ideally through your driver or lodge, and be flexible. Permission depends on the manager and the day's work, and the busy flush seasons in spring are the hardest time. Walking the garden road needs no permission.

faqs.q: What is the best season to see tea plucking?
faqs.a: March to November. First flush, in March and April, is when the most prized tea is made; May and June bring the second flush; the monsoon from June to September has the heaviest plucking. From December to February the bushes are pruned and resting, so there is little activity in the rows.

faqs.q: Is the tea road walk suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are used to walking. The garden road is fairly wide and has little traffic, but parts are steep and the walk back up takes effort. Plan a one-way walk downhill with a car to collect you, and keep children on the road and away from the drop at the edges.

experiences.title: Simana viewpoint and a look into Nepal
experiences.summary: A short drive from Jorepokhri through Sukhia Pokhari to Simana on the Mirik road, where the land drops west into Nepal's Ilam hills and Pashupati market lies just across the border. Best on a clear winter morning.
body: Simana is the Nepali word for border, and that is what it is: a roadside viewpoint on the Sukhia Pokhari to Mirik road where the Indian hills fall away and Nepal begins. Below and to the west roll the hills of Ilam district, known in Nepal for its own tea, with villages and gardens scattered on the slopes. Just across the line is Pashupatinagar, with Pashupati market, where people from both sides come to shop. It is a strange feeling to stand on one ridge and look straight into another country.

From Jorepokhri, drive the 4 km down to Sukhia Pokhari and carry on along the Mirik road to Simana; local cars charge roughly ₹600–1,200 for the return trip with waiting, or you can stop here on the way to Mirik. Clear mornings from October to April give the widest views, and afternoons often haze or cloud over. Tea and snack stalls by the road make it easy to linger over a cup. Take care at the edge of the road, because jeeps come round the curves fast.

Indian citizens usually cross on foot to Pashupati market with valid photo ID such as a voter ID card or passport; no visa is needed. Shops sell clothes, shoes, blankets, packaged food and household goods. Foreign nationals generally cannot use this crossing. Rules, checks and timings change, and border areas can be sensitive, so carry ID, do not photograph security posts and check current status before you travel. If you do not want to cross, the view is reason enough.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a passport to visit Pashupati market?
faqs.a: No visa, and usually no passport. Indian citizens normally cross with valid photo ID such as a passport or voter ID card, and children may need a school ID or birth certificate. Rules and checks change, so carry ID for everyone and check current status before you travel. Foreign nationals generally cannot cross here.

faqs.q: What can we see from Simana viewpoint?
faqs.a: The hills of Ilam district in eastern Nepal, with their tea gardens and villages, and the border settlement of Pashupatinagar just across the line. On clear days the view runs a long way west over ridge after ridge. Morning light from October to April gives the sharpest views; afternoons often haze or cloud over.

faqs.q: Is Simana on the way to Mirik?
faqs.a: Yes. Simana is on the road from Sukhia Pokhari to Mirik, so it is an easy stop on a Darjeeling to Mirik day tour or on the way to an overnight stay in Mirik. Most drivers stop anyway; ask for 20–30 minutes so you can have tea and take in the view.

experiences.title: Where the Himalayan salamander survives now
experiences.duration: Half day to a full day
experiences.best_time: Early monsoon for breeding, by local arrangement
experiences.summary: Follow Jorepokhri's real story: why the Himalayan newt no longer breeds in the sanctuary, and where it survives in village ponds around Sittong and elsewhere. Best done by asking locally, respecting the animal and keeping hands off.
body: The Himalayan salamander, Tylototriton himalayanus, is one of very few tailed amphibians in India. It spends most of the year hidden in damp soil, under stones and in leaf litter, and comes to still pools to breed when the rains arrive, laying eggs on submerged plants. Jorepokhri was protected for it in 1985. Today, according to 2026 reporting by Mongabay, the species is no longer found breeding in the sanctuary, after concrete paving and tourist works altered the ponds it depended on.

It survives elsewhere. The same reporting names ponds such as Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, Pokhritar and Panch Pokhri, several of them on village or private land rather than inside any sanctuary. These are not tourist sites with ticket counters, and the newts are easily disturbed, so the best way to learn more is to ask: at your lodge, among forest staff, or through nature and birding contacts in Darjeeling and Kurseong. If someone offers to take you to a breeding pond in season, go with them and follow their lead.

If you do see a newt, keep your distance. Do not pick it up, move it or shine a torch into the water for long; their skin is delicate and breeding pools are easily disturbed. Do not wade, wash or throw anything into the ponds. Photographs are fine from the bank. And if you want to help, spend your money with village homestays near the breeding ponds, so that keeping the water as it is has a value to the people who live beside it.

faqs.q: Where can we see Himalayan salamanders near Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Not reliably anywhere as a tourist, and not at Jorepokhri, where recent reporting says they no longer breed. Breeding ponds survive at places such as Namthing Pokhri near Sittong, Pokhritar and Panch Pokhri. Ask locally in the breeding season, roughly the early monsoon, and go only with people who know the site.

faqs.q: When do Himalayan salamanders breed?
faqs.a: With the rains, roughly from late spring into the early monsoon, when they gather in still, shallow pools to mate and lay eggs on underwater plants. Timing shifts with the weather each year. Outside that season the adults hide in damp ground and leaf litter and are very hard to find.

faqs.q: Are Himalayan salamanders dangerous?
faqs.a: No. They are small, slow and harmless to people, though like many amphibians their skin carries mild toxins, so wash your hands if you ever touch one by accident. The danger runs the other way: handling, trampling pond edges and pollution harm them. Look, photograph from a distance and leave them alone.

faqs.q: Can we still see salamanders at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: Almost certainly not. Jorepokhri became India's first salamander sanctuary in 1985, but 2026 reporting by Mongabay says concrete paving and tourist works changed the ponds so much that salamanders no longer breed there. The Himalayan newt survives in other ponds, such as Namthing Pokhri near Sittong. Visit Jorepokhri for the forest and the story.

faqs.q: How far is Jorepokhri from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 20 km, roughly an hour by road via Ghoom, Lepchajagat and Sukhia Pokhari; Jorepokhri is about 4 km from Sukhia. A shared jeep to Sukhia costs ₹70–100 a seat, and a local car does the last stretch for ₹400–700 return. A half-day car from Darjeeling costs ₹1,500–2,500.

faqs.q: What does Jorepokhri mean?
faqs.a: Jore pokhri means 'twin ponds' in Nepali, from jor, a pair, and pokhari, a pond. The name describes the two small pools in the forest at the centre of the sanctuary. You will see it written several ways, including Jorepokhri, Jore Pokhri and Jorpokhari, on signs, maps and booking sites.

faqs.q: How do we book Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge?
faqs.a: Through the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration's tourism department, at its office in Darjeeling or through its online booking where available. Rooms are limited and simple. Booking systems and rates change, so check current status before you travel, carry the booking slip and ID, and confirm dinner arrangements in advance.

faqs.q: Is Jorepokhri worth visiting?
faqs.a: As a 30-minute to one-hour stop, yes: the forest ponds are quiet and the story of India's first salamander sanctuary is worth knowing, including its sad turn. As a destination on its own it is small. Combine it with Lepchajagat, Sukhia Pokhari, the Mim tea garden and Simana in a day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: October to early December and March to May bring the clearest, driest days. Winter mornings are cold, close to freezing, but often sunny. From June to September it rains most days and the forest is wrapped in mist, which suits a quiet walk if you have a good rain jacket and do not mind leeches.

faqs.q: Is Jorepokhri good for children?
faqs.a: As a short stop, yes. The path around the ponds is short and easy, and children usually enjoy the forest. Keep them back from the water's edge and explain why touching animals in the ponds is harmful. Pair it with the toy train or the Darjeeling zoo for a fuller family day.

faqs.q: Can we combine Jorepokhri with a Mirik trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Jorepokhri is about 4 km off the Darjeeling to Mirik road at Sukhia Pokhari, and the Simana viewpoint looks into Nepal on the same road. Most Mirik day tours from Darjeeling can add it if you ask. Expect ₹3,000–4,000 for a car for a full day with Lepchajagat, Jorepokhri, Simana and Mirik.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: There may be a small entry or parking fee collected at the site, and the amounts change. Lodge guests are already inside the area. Carry small notes and check current status before you travel, since fees and opening arrangements for sanctuaries and tourist sites in the hills are revised from time to time.
